concept.shortExplanation: Stack neurons into a layer and layers into a network, and each layer gets to reshape the space the next one sees. A problem that no straight line can separate becomes trivially separable once an earlier layer has bent the coordinates. The network in this chapter is real: weights initialised randomly, trained in your browser on a two-dimensional dataset with actual forward and backward passes, no framework involved.
concept.ahaMoment: The last layer is still just drawing a straight line. Everything before it exists to move the data until a straight line is enough.

modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The in-browser network trainer failed to start. Reload the chapter to retry — training happens locally with nothing to download.

levels.title: Separate the Circles
levels.instructions: Concentric rings — no single line will do it. Add a hidden layer, train, and reach the target accuracy. The decision boundary redraws from the network's real outputs as it learns.
hints: One straight line can never separate a ring from what's inside it — you need at least one hidden layer before training will make any real progress.
The default architecture (one hidden layer of 4 units) already has enough capacity for two concentric circles; a higher learning rate just gets you there in fewer epochs.
Leave the architecture at its default (2–4–1), set η ≈ 0.3, and train for around 150 epochs — that reaches 100% validation accuracy.

levels.title: Solve XOR Properly
levels.instructions: The dataset that defeated the perceptron. Find the smallest network that solves it — the score rewards accuracy per parameter, so brute force will not get you three stars.
hints: This is scored per parameter, so before adding units, ask whether XOR actually needs two hidden layers at all — it doesn't need much.
A single hidden layer is enough to solve XOR; the real question is how few units in that one layer still learn it reliably. Fewer parameters at the same accuracy scores strictly better here.

One hidden layer of 3 or 4 units (architecture 2–3–1 or 2–4–1, about 13–17 parameters) trains to roughly 91% accuracy and clears three stars — beating the default two-hidden-layer setup on efficiency even though raw accuracy is similar.

levels.title: The Spiral
levels.instructions: Two interleaved spirals. This needs real depth. Design the architecture, pick the activation, train it, and watch each hidden layer's representation unwind the problem for the next one.
hints: Try the default architecture and just train for a while first — watch whether accuracy is actually climbing or stuck. If it's stuck near 50%, the problem probably isn't the architecture or the epoch budget.

tanh saturates on a network this deep for this dataset — the gradient signal struggles to get back through two hidden tanh layers, so it stalls around 53% accuracy no matter how long you train or what learning rate you pick. Switch the activation instead of fighting it with more epochs.

Keep the default architecture (two hidden layers, 8 units each) but switch the activation to ReLU or leaky ReLU, use η ≈ 0.08, and train the full 900 epochs — that combination reaches essentially 100% accuracy, comfortably past three stars.
